patient.name: Rajesh Patel
patient.complaint: Swollen, red right foot with a discharging ulcer and fever for 4 days
background: Type 2 diabetes for 15 years, HbA1c 82 mmol/mol
Ulcer under the right big toe for 3 months
Taxi driver from Harrow; no known drug allergies

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' or 'Which is the most likely causative organism?': bone pain and fever with a risk factor (diabetic foot ulcer, open fracture, IVDU, sickle cell). S. aureus overall; Salmonella in sickle cell.

points: Rajesh, 58, diabetic: ulcer under his right big toe for **3 months**.
Four days of a **swollen, red foot** and smelly discharge.
Feverish and shivery; little pain because of neuropathy.

steps.lead: Rajesh's ulcer has let bacteria into the bone and marrow beneath: **osteomyelitis**, most likely **Staphylococcus aureus**.
Rajesh has the classic risk factors: **diabetes**, a **chronic foot ulcer** and neuropathy that stopped him noticing it.

points: 2 cm ulcer over the **1st metatarsal head**.
A sterile probe passes down and **touches bone**.
Erythema and swelling over the forefoot.
Reduced monofilament sensation; foot pulses palpable.

steps.lead: Local bone tenderness, swelling, overlying erythema and **fever**: Rajesh's presentation fits, even though neuropathy blunts his pain.

steps.q: Rajesh's ulcer probes to bone and he has a fever. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
steps.r: A diabetic ulcer that **probes to bone** with fever is **osteomyelitis** until proven otherwise. Cellulitis alone does not reach bone.

steps.title: Osteomyelitis in three settings
head: Setting
Usual route
Typical site
Classic organism
rows: Adult with diabetic ulcer or open fracture
Femoral or humeral head, long bones

steps.lead: Rajesh does not have sickle cell. If he did, a hot tender joint and fever would point to **Salmonella** osteomyelitis of the femoral or humeral head.
Rajesh is at risk of **sepsis**, bone destruction and **chronic osteomyelitis**. If a deep abscess forms, antibiotics alone will fail.

steps.text: Do not call a red foot with an ulcer 'just **cellulitis**'. If the ulcer **probes to bone** or the toe looks sausage-like, think osteomyelitis.
Neuropathic patients may have **little pain**. In a diabetic foot, fever, discharge and a raised CRP count for more than the pain score.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' with MRI as the most sensitive early test, X-ray changes appearing later, and bone biopsy as the gold standard that guides antibiotics.

A **bone biopsy** of Rajesh's metatarsal head goes for histology and culture so his antibiotics can be **targeted**.

steps.title: Investigating suspected osteomyelitis
nodes: Bone biopsy: gold standard, guides antibiotics

steps.text: A **superficial ulcer swab** grows skin colonisers and can mislead. The organism that matters comes from **bone biopsy** or blood cultures.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': IV flucloxacillin plus rifampicin for at least 4 weeks, vancomycin for MRSA, clindamycin for penicillin allergy, and surgery for abscess or dead bone.

steps.lead: Rajesh is systemically unwell, so he is treated as **sepsis** first: cultures, fluids, lactate, and IV antibiotics without delay.

steps.q: Which is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic for Rajesh?
steps.r: Empirical osteomyelitis cover is **IV flucloxacillin plus rifampicin** for S. aureus; oral agents alone are not enough initially.

steps.lead: Rajesh starts **IV flucloxacillin and rifampicin**. If biopsy grows **MRSA** he switches to **vancomycin**; with a severe penicillin allergy he would get **clindamycin**.
Rajesh's empirical flucloxacillin and rifampicin regimen follows **local and national antimicrobial guidelines**.

visual.title: Length of antibiotic course
visual.label: Rajesh 6 weeks
visual.caption: IV for a minimum of 4 weeks in the notes, then tailored to complete 4 to 6 weeks.

points: Day 5: still febrile, pus still discharging.

steps.lead: Rajesh's **deep abscess** needs **surgical drainage** and debridement; antibiotics cannot reach a walled-off pus collection.

visual.title: Rajesh's CRP on treatment
visual.caption: CRP barely fell on antibiotics alone; it fell steadily once the abscess was drained.

steps.lead: If Rajesh's infection became **chronic**, antibiotics would **wait for sensitivities** from bone samples, usually alongside surgery.

steps.title: Osteomyelitis management
nodes: Abscess or dead bone → surgical drainage / debridement
Total course 4 to 6 weeks, IV then tailored

steps.text: Fusidic acid can replace rifampicin, but **rifampicin is never used alone**: resistance develops quickly. It is always a partner drug.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why children get metaphyseal infection, why sickle cell links to Salmonella, why MRI beats X-ray early, and why sequestra need surgery.

steps.lead: Rajesh's infection came by **direct inoculation** from his ulcer. A child would more likely seed the **metaphysis** through the bloodstream.
S. aureus **biofilm** on Rajesh's bone shields bacteria from antibiotics and immune cells, which is why his course is weeks long.
Untreated, Rajesh could form a **sequestrum** walled in by **involucrum**: dead bone that antibiotics in the blood cannot reach, so it must be removed.

steps.q: Why did Rajesh's MRI show infection when his X-ray did not?
o: MRI detects marrow oedema before cortical loss
steps.r: MRI picks up **bone marrow oedema** early; X-ray needs enough **cortical destruction** to show, which takes longer.

steps.lead: Marrow oedema in Rajesh's metatarsal appears long before the cortex is eroded enough for an X-ray to show it.
In sickle cell disease, gut **vaso-occlusion** lets **Salmonella** translocate into blood, and infarcted bone is fertile ground for it to seed.

steps.text: Children's **metaphyses** have a rich blood supply with **sluggish flow** in looping vessels, so circulating bacteria settle there.

mcq.r: **Salmonella** is the characteristic organism in sickle cell disease.

mcq.r: The **metaphysis**: rich blood supply and sluggish flow.

mcq.r: X-ray changes are a **later** finding; an early X-ray may be normal.

mcq.q: Which is the empirical antibiotic regimen for osteomyelitis?
mcq.r: **IV flucloxacillin + rifampicin** (fusidic acid can replace rifampicin), minimum 4 weeks.

o: A collection of pus under the periosteum

glossary.Osteomyelitis: Infection of bone and bone marrow.
glossary.Staphylococcus aureus: A Gram-positive coccus in clusters; the commonest cause of osteomyelitis.
glossary.MRSA: Meticillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, resistant to flucloxacillin; treated with vancomycin.
glossary.Salmonella: Gram-negative gut bacteria; the characteristic cause of osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease.
glossary.Sickle cell disease: Inherited haemoglobin disorder in which red cells sickle and block small vessels.
glossary.Vaso-occlusion: Blockage of small blood vessels, as by sickled red cells, causing tissue infarction.
glossary.Metaphysis: The flared part of a long bone between the shaft and the growth plate.
glossary.Diaphysis: The shaft of a long bone.
glossary.Epiphysis: The end of a long bone, beyond the growth plate.
glossary.Direct inoculation: Bacteria introduced straight into tissue by injury, surgery or an adjacent ulcer.
glossary.Contiguous spread: Infection spreading from neighbouring tissue, such as a foot ulcer into bone.
glossary.Open fracture: A fracture where the bone communicates with the outside through a wound.
glossary.Sinus tract: A channel from infected tissue to the skin surface that discharges pus.
glossary.Probe to bone: Bedside test: a sterile probe touching bone through an ulcer strongly suggests osteomyelitis.
glossary.Peripheral neuropathy: Nerve damage, often from diabetes, causing numbness so injuries go unnoticed.
glossary.Monofilament: A thin nylon filament pressed on the foot to test protective sensation.
glossary.Charcot neuroarthropathy: Destructive joint disease of the neuropathic foot, giving a warm, swollen, deformed foot.
glossary.Periosteum: The tough membrane covering the outer surface of bone.
glossary.Periosteal reaction: New bone laid down by lifted periosteum, seen on X-ray as a later sign.
glossary.Periosteal elevation: Lifting of the periosteum by pus or oedema, seen early on MRI.
glossary.Bone marrow oedema: Excess fluid in the marrow, an early MRI sign of osteomyelitis.
glossary.Cortical destruction: Erosion of the hard outer bone layer, visible on X-ray later in infection.
glossary.Subperiosteal collection: Fluid or pus trapped beneath the periosteum, visible on ultrasound.
glossary.Bone biopsy: Sampling bone tissue for histology and culture; the gold standard in osteomyelitis.
glossary.Flucloxacillin: A penicillin active against non-MRSA Staphylococcus aureus.
glossary.Rifampicin: An antibiotic with good bone and biofilm penetration, always used with a partner drug.
glossary.Fusidic acid: An anti-staphylococcal antibiotic that can replace rifampicin as a partner drug.
glossary.Vancomycin: An IV glycopeptide antibiotic used for MRSA.
glossary.Clindamycin: An antibiotic with good bone penetration, used in severe penicillin allergy.
glossary.Debridement: Surgical removal of dead or infected tissue.
glossary.Biofilm: A slimy layer of bacteria stuck to a surface, shielded from antibiotics and immune cells.
glossary.Adhesins: Bacterial surface proteins that let bacteria stick to host tissues.
glossary.Sequestrum: A fragment of dead, infected bone in chronic osteomyelitis.
glossary.Involucrum: A sheath of new reactive bone that forms around a sequestrum.
glossary.Sepsis: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated response to infection.
glossary.IVDU: Intravenous drug use, a risk factor for vertebral osteomyelitis.
glossary.HbA1c: Glycated haemoglobin, showing average blood glucose over about 3 months.

technique.stem: A 65 year old man has a 2 week history of pain in his right shin. He had an open fracture of the right tibia fixed surgically 3 months ago. His temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg. The skin over the scar is red and tender. Investigations: X-ray tibia: bony lesion consistent with osteomyelitis.
technique.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?

steps.x: An organism question: check for a special setting such as sickle cell.
Post-traumatic, post-surgical osteomyelitis; no sickle cell, no special host.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Default organism: **Staphylococcus aureus**.

elim: E. coli is a urinary and neonatal organism, not the usual bone pathogen.
Pseudomonas is classic after a puncture through a trainer sole.
Salmonella is the sickle cell answer.
Strep pyogenes causes cellulitis more than osteomyelitis.

steps.x: **D. Staphylococcus aureus.** Rule: osteomyelitis = S. aureus unless the stem says sickle cell.

technique.stem: A 60 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has a 5 day history of a swollen, red left foot with a discharging ulcer over the 2nd metatarsal head. A probe passed through the ulcer touches bone. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. An X-ray of the foot shows soft tissue swelling only.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

steps.x: Next investigation after a normal X-ray when osteomyelitis is suspected.
High suspicion of osteomyelitis; X-ray is still normal early.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **MRI**: the most sensitive early test.

elim: CT is less sensitive than MRI for early marrow change.
Waiting 2 weeks delays diagnosis and treatment.
Ultrasound is used for subperiosteal collections, mainly in children.
Wound swabs grow colonisers, not the bone organism.

steps.x: **B. MRI of the foot.** Rule: normal early X-ray + suspicion = MRI.

technique.stem: A 45 year old man has acute osteomyelitis of the left tibia. He had anaphylaxis to penicillin as a child. His temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg. Blood cultures are taken.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?

steps.x: Antibiotic choice: look for an allergy or MRSA.
Severe penicillin allergy rules out every penicillin.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Clindamycin**.

elim: Amoxicillin is a penicillin.
Benzylpenicillin is a penicillin.
Co-amoxiclav contains amoxicillin.
Flucloxacillin is a penicillin.

steps.x: **C. Clindamycin.** Rule: severe penicillin allergy = clindamycin; MRSA = vancomycin.

technique.stem: A 40 year old man has had a discharging sinus over his right tibia for 2 years since an open fracture. X-ray shows a dense fragment of dead bone surrounded by a shell of new bone. Despite several long courses of antibiotics the discharge persists.
technique.q: Which is the most likely reason antibiotics have failed?
o: Avascular dead bone shields the bacteria

steps.x: A mechanism question: why does chronic osteomyelitis resist antibiotics?
Sequestrum (dead bone) inside involucrum (new bone).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The **sequestrum** has no blood supply, so antibiotics cannot reach the bacteria: surgery is needed.

elim: Resistance is possible but does not explain the dead bone picture.
Marrow hyperplasia is a haematological finding, not this.
Low density is osteoporosis.
Osteoblasts are active: they made the involucrum.

steps.x: **B. Avascular dead bone shields bacteria.** Rule: sequestrum = surgery.

practice.stem: A 9 year old boy has a 3 day history of pain above his left knee and a limp. He has been feverish. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 104/62 mmHg. There is marked tenderness over the distal femur just above the knee. The knee joint has a full range of passive movement without pain.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Fever, raised markers and focal tenderness over the distal femoral metaphysis with a freely moving knee is acute osteomyelitis. Septic arthritis would make joint movement very painful.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a febrile child with leg pain.

clues: full range of passive movement without pain
steps.x: Metaphyseal tenderness, fever, joint itself spared.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Haematogenous **acute osteomyelitis** of the metaphysis.

elim: Ewing's is a more gradual course with night pain; fever this acute favours infection.
Osteosarcoma is a slow painful mass, not acute fever.
Septic arthritis makes any joint movement exquisitely painful.
Transient synovitis has low fever, normal markers and hip involvement.

steps.x: **A. Acute osteomyelitis.** Rule: febrile child + metaphyseal tenderness + free joint = osteomyelitis.

practice.stem: A 23 year old man with sickle cell disease has a 4 day history of pain in his right shin and fever. His temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg. Investigations: X-ray tibia: bony lesion consistent with osteomyelitis.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Salmonella is the characteristic cause of osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease, because gut vaso-occlusion allows translocation into the blood.

steps.x: Organism: look for a special host.
Sickle cell + osteomyelitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Salmonella** species.

elim: H. influenzae is a respiratory organism, rare in bone now.
Pseudomonas follows puncture wounds through footwear.
Strep pyogenes causes cellulitis and pharyngitis.
Treponema causes syphilis.

steps.x: **C. Salmonella species.** Rule: sickle cell + bone infection = Salmonella.

practice.stem: A 62 year old woman with type 2 diabetes and peripheral neuropathy has a 6 week history of an ulcer under her right great toe. The toe is now red, swollen and sausage-shaped. A sterile probe passed through the ulcer touches bone. Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 140/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A diabetic ulcer that probes to bone with a sausage toe, fever and high ESR is osteomyelitis. Cellulitis does not reach bone.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a diabetic foot problem.
Chronic ulcer, sausage toe, positive probe to bone, raised ESR.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Osteomyelitis** of the phalanx or metatarsal.

elim: Cellulitis does not explain probe to bone.
Charcot gives a hot swollen deformed midfoot, often without an ulcer or fever.
Gout gives an acute hot joint, not a probe-to-bone ulcer.
Probe touching bone means bone is involved.

steps.x: **E. Osteomyelitis.** Rule: diabetic ulcer probes to bone = osteomyelitis.

practice.stem: A 34 year old man who injects heroin has a 3 week history of worsening low back pain, night sweats and fevers. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 122/74 mmHg. There is marked tenderness on percussion over L3. Lower limb power, sensation and reflexes are normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Back pain with fever, raised markers and focal spinal percussion tenderness in an IV drug user is vertebral osteomyelitis. Neurological symptoms are not typical.

steps.x: Diagnosis of back pain with red flags.
IVDU, fever, focal spinal tenderness, no neuro deficit.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Haematogenous **vertebral osteomyelitis**.

elim: AS is inflammatory back pain in young men without fever.
Mechanical pain does not cause fever and a CRP of 124.
Metastases need a primary and give no fever.
Wedge fractures are osteoporotic, after minor trauma.

steps.x: **D. Vertebral osteomyelitis.** Rule: IVDU + fever + spinal tenderness = vertebral osteomyelitis.

practice.stem: A 7 year old girl has a 2 day history of pain in her right shin and fever. An X-ray of the tibia is normal. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 120 bpm and BP 100/60 mmHg. Osteomyelitis of the proximal tibial metaphysis is suspected and an MRI is performed.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on MRI?
o: Bone marrow oedema with periosteal elevation
Lytic lesion with onion-skin periosteal reaction
practice.e: Early osteomyelitis shows bone marrow oedema and periosteal elevation on MRI before X-ray changes. Onion-skin is Ewing's; soap bubble is giant cell tumour.

steps.x: Expected MRI finding in early osteomyelitis.

clues: X-ray of the tibia is normal
steps.x: Very early infection: X-ray is still normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bone marrow oedema** and periosteal elevation.

elim: Chondrocalcinosis is pseudogout.
Onion-skin periosteal reaction is Ewing's sarcoma.
MRI is sensitive early, so it should be abnormal.
Soap bubble is a giant cell tumour.

steps.x: **A. Marrow oedema with periosteal elevation.** Rule: MRI sees oedema before X-ray sees destruction.

practice.stem: A 48 year old man had an open fracture of his left tibia 3 years ago. For the past year he has had intermittent discharge of pus from a small opening over the shin. His temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 130/82 mmHg. X-ray shows a dense fragment of bone surrounded by new bone formation.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A discharging sinus years after an open fracture, with a sequestrum surrounded by involucrum, is chronic osteomyelitis.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a long-standing problem after an open fracture.

clues: dense fragment of bone surrounded by new bone
steps.x: Sinus tract, sequestrum, involucrum, low-grade CRP.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Chronic osteomyelitis**.

elim: Acute osteomyelitis is days to weeks, with high fever.
Ewing's affects children and young adults, with onion-skin reaction.

Septic arthritis involves a joint, not the shin.

steps.x: **B. Chronic osteomyelitis.** Rule: sinus + sequestrum + involucrum = chronic.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man has a 3 day history of severe pain in his right lower leg 2 weeks after a tibial plateau fracture was fixed. steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

practice.stem: A 64 year old man with diabetes has osteomyelitis of the right foot. After 5 days of IV flucloxacillin he still has fever, a persistent purulent discharge and deep tenderness of the sole. His temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 130/76 mmHg. MRI shows a deep plantar collection.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
practice.e: A deep abscess in a diabetic foot with persistent discharge despite flucloxacillin needs surgical drainage. Changing antibiotics will not clear walled-off pus.

Failure of antibiotics because of an abscess.

practice.stem: A 59 year old man is on IV flucloxacillin and rifampicin for osteomyelitis of the left tibia. Bone biopsy culture grows Staphylococcus aureus resistant to meticillin. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 90 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate change to his antibiotics?
practice.e: Meticillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) on bone biopsy is treated with vancomycin. Clindamycin is the choice in severe penicillin allergy.

MRSA confirmed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Vancomycin**.

elim: Clindamycin is for severe penicillin allergy, not the MRSA choice in the notes.
Co-amoxiclav does not cover MRSA.

practice.stem: An 8 year old boy has acute osteomyelitis of the distal femoral metaphysis with no history of trauma. Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. His temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 116 bpm and BP 102/64 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely reason the infection settled in the metaphysis?
o: Rich blood supply with sluggish flow
practice.e: Haematogenous bacteria seed the metaphysis because it has a rich vascular supply with sluggish flow in looping vessels.

steps.x: Mechanism: why the metaphysis?
Haematogenous spread in a child.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Rich blood supply with sluggish flow** lets bacteria settle.

elim: The metaphysis has periosteum.
Osteoclast activity does not trap bacteria.
The metaphysis contains marrow.
Articular cartilage is at the epiphysis, not the metaphysis.
